cues.text: Start with the embryogenesis board.
A shows a globular embryo, with a simplified suspensor below it.
B shows the heart shaped stage, where two cotyledon primordia create the
familiar outline.
This is not an animal heart or evidence of a plant circulatory organ.
The embryo develops from the zygote, whereas the embryo sac is the female
gametophyte present before fertilisation.
They are not alternative names for one structure.
The drawing omits surrounding endosperm and maternal tissues so that the
changing embryo shape remains clear.
It represents a selected dicot pattern, not an exact developmental timetable
for every flowering plant.
C shows the elongated torpedo stage and D a selected cotyledonary embryo with
two cotyledons and an organised axis.
Read A, B, C and D as the sequence.
Do not treat drawing size or the distance between panels as a growth rate.
The suspensor supports the developing embryo and is a temporary developmental
structure, rather than the mature seedling's primary root.
Detailed cell contributions to the root pole are not mapped in this schematic.
Embryo maturation establishes the body plan before germination, but organ
growth and differentiation continue afterwards.
A seedling is therefore not formed merely by unfolding a perfectly complete
miniature adult plant.
The second board shows three selected stages.
Panel one is a dry seed.
Panel two represents water uptake, or imbibition, and qualitative swelling.
Panel three shows emergence of the radicle through an opening in the coat.
Water uptake supports rehydration and renewed metabolic activity, but swelling
alone does not prove that a seed is alive or able to establish a seedling.
Non living dry materials can also absorb water.
The drawn size difference is not a measured volume ratio, and no number of
hours is supplied.
Keep the physical uptake of water separate from the later evidence of active
embryo growth.
The radicle is the embryonic root region, and its emergence is a common
visible
marker used to describe germination.
Establishment of a healthy seedling requires more than this first protrusion.
Suitable water, oxygen and temperature usually matter, while light
requirements
vary among species.
More water is not always better: saturated conditions can restrict oxygen
supply.
A viable dormant seed may fail to germinate even when otherwise favourable
conditions are provided; that differs from a non dormant seed waiting because
its environment is unsuitable.
This board does not test a seed lot or prescribe one universal laboratory
protocol.
Read the visible event without claiming every requirement has been measured.
Use the common bean comparison.
The dashed horizontal line marks the soil surface.
In the later right panel, the pair of cotyledons is above this line because
elongation of the hypocotyl has raised their attachment level.
This is epigeal germination in the selected common bean example.
The shoot and its young leaves lie above the cotyledons, while roots extend
below the soil.
Do not call the raised cotyledons the first true leaves merely because both
may
appear green.
They differ in developmental identity.
The two panels are selected stages rather than a complete animation of the
protective hypocotyl hook or a measured growth experiment.
Interpret the common bean board using the cotyledonary node rather than simply
noticing that roots grow downward.
Roots also grow below ground in the pea comparison.
What distinguishes the selected epigeal pattern is the raised cotyledons.
Cotyledons can supply stored reserves and, in some seedlings, later contribute
photosynthetically, but a line drawing does not measure either contribution.
They may eventually shrink or fall as reserves are used and the seedling
develops.
This common bean example should not be extended to every species with bean in
its common name.
Identify the structural pattern first, then apply the stated example.
The pea board uses the same soil reference.
In its later panel, the cotyledons remain below the surface while the
epicotyl,
above their attachment level, elongates into the emerged shoot.
This is the selected hypogeal pattern.
The hypocotyl does not raise the cotyledonary node as in common bean.
Trace the stem down from the visible leaves to the underground cotyledons
rather than confusing those leaves with cotyledons that have moved upward.
The roots extend below the seed region.
This schematic omits details such as seed coat shedding and the full emergence
sequence, and it supplies no clock or numerical elongation rate.
Finish by comparing the two germination boards.
Common bean and pea both have dicot embryos, yet the selected examples differ
in whether cotyledons rise above the soil.
Epigeal versus hypogeal is therefore not simply another name for dicot versus
monocot.
In common bean, hypocotyl elongation raises the cotyledons; in pea, epicotyl
elongation raises the shoot while cotyledons remain below.
Keep the soil reference consistent and identify the attachment level before
deciding.
Neither drawing gives the percentage of a seed batch that germinates or
survives.
Those require observations, counts and a stated method rather than one
idealised seedling.
